Dealer Is Selling a Corvette ZR1X for $400,000 Over Sticker, Calls It by a Name That Doesn't Exist
12 photos
Photo: Abomination | X
A couple of photos have been making the rounds on the internet, taking the auto world by surprise. A dealership in Arkansas listed a 2027 Chevrolet Corvette ZR1X with a $400,000 markup, calling it exclusive and naming it "Flagship Hypercar Edition," something that doesn't even exist.
The photos show how George Nunnally Chevrolet in Arkansas listed a 2027 Corvette ZR1X for sale with an unbelievable dealer markup , raising the asking price from the $296,445 MSRP all the way to a mind-blowing $696,445.
For the money, you could buy a Lamborghini Revuelto plug-in hybrid and still have money left for a Corvette Stingray. However, the dealership obviously got its hands on a motorized "treasure" and will by no means let it go without a fight. Or a markup. Or whatever.
The dealer tried to justify the extra money asked for the car, calling it the Flagship Hypercar Edition, which is not an actual edition, but a fabricated and absurd way of trying to artificially make the price of the ZR1X go through the roof.
Photo: Abomination | X The dealership refers to the silly markup as an "Exclusive Market Value Adjustment” and "Hypercar Demand Premium," and mentions "Extreme Exclusivity." True, it is an exclusive hypercar with zero inventory, being produced only on demand and coming with long waiting times.
Because production numbers are extremely tight and individual dealer allocations are rare, the vehicle has become a prime target for inflated dealership pricing and secondary car market flipping despite the 12-month resale ban imposed by General Motors through the purchase contract.
However, while General Motors heavily punishes flippers by voiding factory warranties if the cars are sold during the first year of ownership, it allows authorized dealerships to tack on a 135% markup with no problem whatsoever.
The Corvette ZR1X that the dealership in Arkansas is trying to sell rolled off the production line of the Bowling Green Assembly Plant in Kentucky with the 3LZ package . It is finished in the show-stopping Red Mist Metallic paint over a Jet Black interior.
Photo: Chevrolet With everything it's got on it, it would have dropped right under the $300,000 mark. For the money, customers willing to wait for months would get the exotic hypercar powered by the mighty twin-turbocharged 5.5-liter V8 and the front-mounted electric motor, pushing out a mind-blowing 1,250 horsepower (1,267 metric horsepower) and 973 pound-feet (1,320 Newton meters) of torque.
That is enough for the Corvette ZR1X to rocket from 0 to 60 mph (0 to 97 kph) in 1.89 seconds and run the quarter mile in 8.99 seconds, and max out at 233 mph (375 kph). After all, it is the car that lapped the Nürburgring in an incredible 6 minutes and 49.275 seconds, which makes it the second fastest American production car in the Green Hell.
Early listings and auctions have shown cars changing hands for anywhere between $312,000 and $550,000; George Nunally’s near-$700,000 is definitely an absurdity. The dealership probably expected this car to be sold quietly. Now, the whole internet knows about the dealer markup record. At the end of the day, the ZR1X is still a Chevy!
Other models that hit the market with massive dealer markups The Chevrolet Corvette ZR1X is by no means the only car that hit the market with massive dealer markups. Remember that the Tesla Cybertruck, which now has its days numbered, was there, too, back in late 2023 and early 2024, when it finally launched.
There was a time when a Porsche dealership listed the electric pickup truck for $249,000 when the starting price of the Foundation Series was around $100,000. In the meantime, Tesla tried to hunt down the flippers but gloriously failed.
Photo: Dodge 2023 was one Hell(cat) of a year for the car market. It was the year Dodge rolled out the Challenger SRT Demon 170 with 1,025 horsepower (1,039 metric horsepower). Dealerships routinely added markups between $100,000 and $250,000, despite Dodge trying to prioritize allocations to dealerships that promised to sell at sticker price.
Limited-run Porsche models have also been subject to markups over the years. The 911 Sport Classic saw markups as high as $250,000, while standard GT3 variants often see $100,000 tacked onto their $160,000 sticker prices.
It was the same for the Ford F-150 Lightning when it launched back in April 2022. The demand was so huge that dealerships wanted to ride the wave of popularity, prompting dealers to add $30,000 to $50,000 "market adjustments." In the meantime, Ford pulled the plug on the once-very-popular electric truck.
General Motors has been through this before, time and again. For instance, the early production GMC Hummer EV Edition 1 models were sold by dealers for $100,000+ over their original six-figure MSRP, with listings showing prices north of $250,000.
GM kept its distance back then, just like it did with the ZR1 without the X or the Z06. But now, it's maybe time it interfered. This Chevy dealer wants $400,000 over sticker for a Zr1x lmao https://t.co/bDhJKZ9iqY — Abomination (@Abomination81) October 30, 2026
